div.p: Preemption is a key factor against architectural coupling in concurrent systems. The whole verification process of real-time systems postulates composability in multiple di mensions, including time. As coupling wrecks composabil ity, the design of real-time systems really needs preemption. However preemption effects complicate feasibility analysis or make it more pessimistic. Hence methods that limit pre emptions without affecting feasibility are attractive. State of-the-art approaches to limited preemption, however, do not treat resource sharing with the importance that it de serves. The placement of non-preemptive regions -and their interactions with shared resources -should not become a design problem, but rather stay as an implementation level feature that does not backtrack to the design space. In this paper we present a refinement to the state-of-the-art lim ited preemption model that addresses the interaction with resource sharing, and discuss a kernel implementation that uses run-time knowledge to warrant safe and efficient over laps between critical sections and non-preemptive regions. Experimental results prove the effectiveness of the proposed solution.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Incrementality is a distinctive and unifying trait of the in dustrial software development process: design, development, 978-1-4799-1443-2/13/$3l.00 ©2013 IEEE integration and qualification proceed in incremental steps to better master the complexity of increasingly large and heterogeneous systems. The viability of such a divide-and conquer approach silently builds on the principle of compos ability, which promises that the properties ascertained on a given build are preserved upon composition with other mod ules up until the system is final. In hard real-time systems, where timeliness plays a prominent role, composability is expected to go beyond the functional dimension, to enable separate timing analysis on smaller, functionally cohesive building blocks that could be tasks or groups thereof. Time composability should guarantee that the timing behaviour of any such building block is not inordinately affected by the presence and activity of any other task in that system. State-of-the-art schedulability analysis approaches, such as e. g. Response Time Analysis (RTA) [17], assume that dis turbance can be safely bounded. The soundness itself of the analysis results critically depends on the actual degree of time composability in the system.

The use of advanced hardware features, including cache hierarchies, complex pipelines and branch predictors, to speed up the execution in modern architectures exposes the sys tem to execution time jitter because the very operation of those processor resources depends on recent history of execu tion [22]. History-sensitive execution-time jitter wrecks time composability among tasks in so far as task interleaving and interactions cause interference on the hardware state, thence on their own timing behavior. This phenomenon, though more evident in multi-processor systems, equally applies to comparatively simpler single-processor platforms. Unless we want to resort to a simplified (and less performing) hard ware architecture, as proposed in [18], time composability is in danger. Timing interferences must otherwise be taken into account in more complex forms of schedulability anal ysis; for example the interference of caches on task inter leaving is considered in [1]. Yet the cumulative interference arising from all history-sensitive hardware cannot always be efficiently accounted for by state-of-the-art timing analysis techniques, short of risking excessive pessimism.

An alternative approach consists in trying to reduce inter task interference by focusing on task preemption as its main root source. In that light, a reduction in the number of preemptions that can be experienced by each job of a task directly incurs a reduction in the amount of possible inter ference. Several approaches have been proposed to limitor even altogether avoid -the occurrence of preemption, while at the same time preserving the feasibility of the task set [4,10,13]. Those methods fall under the umbrella term of limited preemptive scheduling.

Most existing approaches, however, rely on the simplify ing assumption of task independence and seem not to make much of the fact that real systems often include shared re sources which multiple tasks can access in mutual exclusion. Shared resources are often explicitly ignored in the proposed models or, when mentioned, are simplistically assumed to be encapsulated within non-preemptive chunks of execution. In real-world systems, instead, shared resources are a fun damental enabler to functional decoupling and predictable synchronization patterns among tasks. As such, they convey design-level constraints that cannot be disregard or handled retrospectively in a limited preemption scheme that aspires to be industrially relevant.

In this paper we address single-processor systems and fo cus on the potential benefits to time composability that can be obtained from applying a limited preemption model and identify the most promising approach in term of interference reduction and industrial applicability. We provide a moti vating example showing how the simplifying assumptions expressed by existing methods on shared resources may eas ily fail in practice and cause an otherwise feasible task set to become infeasible. On account of the lack of adequate support, we extend the selected approach to account for the presence of shared resources in the system. We then support our reasoning by providing an implementation of a limited preemption model on a real operating system and provide an experimental evaluation thereof, with respect to both inter ference reduction and effective implementation of a shared resource access protocol.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Sec tion 2 surveys the existing approaches in the area of limited preemption; Section 3 provides a motivation of our work and introduces preliminary concepts and notations; Section 4 introduces our model extension and discusses how it is ex pected to cope with shared resources; Section 5 presents a concrete implementation of our model and reports an exper imental evaluation of our approach; Section 6, finally, draws some conclusions.

div.head: RELATED WORK
div.p: The idea of limiting preemptions to reduce interference caused to the task set and increase schedulability is not new to scheduling theory. Inhibiting preemption altogether is not an option for those system whose feasibility must be strictly guaranteed as the optimality results obtained for fixed-priority preemptive scheduling do not hold any more [16]. This observation motivates a recently increasing inter est towards less restrictive approaches aiming at finding a compromise between reducing the effects of preemption and preserving schedulability of a task set [13,28]. In deferred preemption approaches in particular the emphasis is placed on the fact that preemption requests are not immediately served but may be rather deferred (i.e. postponed) for some period of time.

Preemption deferral mechanisms have the practical ef fect of splitting the execution of each task in preemptible and non-preemptible parts. Non-preemptive regions (NPR), within which preemption cannot take place, are either de termined by fixed points in the task code or triggered by specific scheduling or timing events. The former approach is indeed exploited by one of the first attempts to intro duce deferred preemptions within a fixed-priority scheduling scheme (FPDS), described by Burns in [11]: the cited work proposes a cooperative scheduling approach, where each task should explicitly request to be preempted by invoking a yield routine in the kernel. Although blocking time effect stem ming from preemption deferral was incorporated in refined response-time equations, this seminal work did not address the problem of computing the maximum allowable length of non-preemptive chunks.

More recently, Bril et al. [9,10] improved this model by showing that current analysis was not precise, i. e. it can be either optimistic or pessimistic according to the specific scenario; the cited authors proved that in the general FPDS case the worst-case response time of a task cannot be calcu lated by only looking at its first job, since the delay intro duced by the last non-preemptive chunk of a task on higher priority jobs may indirectly delay its subsequent job acti vations (a phenomenon known as self-pushing). To address this problem the authors used the notion of level-i active period and refined the analysis to account for it. Yao et al. showed in [29,30] that no self-pushing can occur under the fixed preemptions point (FPP) model if two favourable conditions are met: (i) the task set has con strained deadlines; and (ii) it is preemptively feasible. Un fortunately, the FPP approach suffers drawbacks that make its adoption impractical in real-world scenarios. Preemp tion points should be explicitly programmed into applica tion code, which is hard to do in the presence of legacy code, and their placement needs to be reconsidered every time a new task is added to the system, thus making the approach unsuitable for systems that may change over time. Additionally, the choice of preemption points placement is a challenge in itself, which as such has been addressed in some works with the specific goal of increasing system schedula bility [6] or of minimizing preemption overhead [7].

Alternative and more flexible approaches instead imple ment non-preemptive regions without relying upon their ex plicit position in the code so that NPRS are said to be float ing in the code. Since there is no explicit positioning, NPRs should be initiated at a certain time stamp or in response to some kind of event as, for example, the activation of a higher priority task (i. e. , activation-triggered approach). In floating NPR approaches the only relevant issue is thus to determine the maximum admissible length of a floating NPR that preserve feasibility of the system. This challenge has been tackled by Yao et al. in [27] for FPS and by Baruah [4] for EDF; more recently, Davis and Bertogna [14] have de vised an algorithm to compute both NPR length and a task priority assignment which preserves schedulability. These works all assume job arrival at their critical instant to en sure safety of the analysis: however, when job phasing is introduced in the task set, the length of NPRS can be further extended with respect to the worst-case scenario of simulta neous job releases, as explained in [20].

To the best of our knowledge no real-world implemen tation of a limited-preemptive scheduler exists and the va lidity of published results has been proven by simulation only. Some initial considerations on implementation issues are given in [21] and [5], for the mechanism of ready-queue locking and for memory occupancy and resource sharing, respectively. Marinho et al. [19] have also investigated the beneficial effects on the cache-related preemption delay suf fered by each task under a NPR scheme, as a function of the reduced number of preemptions. In this paper we focus on limiting the number of preemptions in the presence of shared resources without discriminating on the actual and specific cost of a preemptions.

An alternative yet valid approach for limiting the effects of preemption is the Preemption Threshold (PTS) method introduced by Wang and Saksena [23,26]: although the au thors showed that schedulability can be improved by PTS, difficulties arise in the choice of thresholds. Since preemp tion is still enabled in PTS, this scheduling technique can be have exactly as fully preemptive or non-preemptive schedul ing according to the specific threshold tuning, which is there fore crucial to achieve desired results. However, none of these works consider the presence of shared resources explicitly: they either ignore them or as sume that no preemption can occur within them. Of course, this assumption does not hold in the general case and may be violated in the presence of non-preemptive regions whose placement is unknown at design time. This work is there fore the first attempt to evaluate the limited-preemptive ap proach on a real kernel and to cope in the kernel design with the interactions between resource-related and preemption related blocking simultaneously.

div.head: RESOURCES
div.p: The assumption of task independence, which has often been put forward to allow an easier mathematical formu lation of the schedulability analysis problem, rarely holds for real systems. Tasks routinely share physical and logical resources as a means to cater for collaborative goals.

In fully preemptive systems, shared resources typically need to be accessed in mutual exclusion so that data consis tency is preserved across accesses. As a result of serializing accesses, a task may be blocked as it tries to access a resource that is already in use by a lower priority task and thus may need to wait for the latter to relinquish the resource. In this case, the system is vulnerable to either potentially un bounded priority inversion or risk of deadlock. The use of an appropriate resource access protocol can prevent deadlock and establish a bound to the duration of priority inversion.

Limited preemption scheduling arguably mitigates the prob lem of providing safe accesses to shared resources. At one end of the spectrum of limited preemption approaches, for totally non-preemptive systems, mutual exclusion, priority inversion and deadlock do not pose any threat as resources are not concurrently accessed any more. While providing clear advantages in terms of time composability, disabling preemption may reduce system feasibility 1 and cannot al ways assure the required responsiveness for critical tasks. In less restrictive approaches, the problem of shared resource accesses is not avoided a priori but assumed to be solved by enforcing proper nesting of critical sections within non preemptive execution chunks. This assumption, however, is only viable in static approaches where preemption points can be selected ad-hoc to include access to shared resources. The identification of fixed preemption points for all tasks in a system is a most undesirable obligation, also scarcely scalable to real-world systems.
As noted in Section 2, the confinement of all shared re-1 Some task sets that are infeasible under rate monotonic scheduling are indeed schedulable in non-preemptive mode and vice-versa [14].

In the activation-triggered de ferred preemption approach, for example, the analysis model does not tell the exact position of preemption points, and the boundaries of a non-preemptive region depend on run time events such as the activation of higher priority tasks.

In this case the safeness of the model cannot be guaranteed and the schedulability of a task set may be compromised un less some sort of countermeasure is taken. This eventuality is confirmed by a simple motivating example involving the synthetic task set reported in Table 1, consisting in three periodic tasks {T1' T2, T3 } with total utilization U = 0.872.

We regard the activation-triggered model as the most promis ing variant of the deferred preemption approach as it achieves a good compromise between effectiveness and applicability. This model in fact allows taking benefit of the slack in a system without imposing any restrictive design choices on the system designer: any decision is in fact deferred to run time. On the other hand, however, the activation-triggered deferred preemption model alone cannot prevent harmful overlap of NPRs with critical sections.

In the following we reason on the relationships between shared resources and NPRs. We elaborate on a possible ap proach to reconcile mutual exclusion and limited preemp tion, based on an extension to the deferred preemption model, further refined by means of run-time countermeasure. As a preliminary step, we first recall the terminology and formal characterization of both the deferred preemption model and most common resource access protocols.

div.head: HANDLING SHARED RESOURCES
div.p: Previous studies on deferred preemption neglect the diffi culties of the coexistence of NPRS and shared resources. In most cases (e. g., [6,13,14]) this challenge has been solved by assuming proper nesting of critical sections within non preemptive execution chunks. This assumption, however, may be difficult to enforce in real systems, either because all resource access patterns (nested accesses included) must be taken into account, which may be too labour intensive and error prone, or because the model itself does not allow controlling the exact boundaries of non preemptive regions.

As observed in Section 3, this work addresses the activation triggered approach which exploits floating non-preemptive regions. According to this model, a NPR of a task Ti starts with the (first) activation of a higher priority task T j E T/ and finishes exactly after qjax units of execution. div.head: Run-time support
div.p: The proposed extensions to the activation-triggered model are not fully satisfactory from the time composability stand point. In cases @ and Q in Figure 2 the pessimism caused by the need to support ICPP brings in additional and not always necessary preemptions, which is against our main motivation. Better results can be obtained by exploiting run-time knowledge to reduce the pessimism in the model. To this end, low-level support from the underlying operating system is required.

div.head: EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION
div.p: The reduction in the amount of preemptions in a system is the benefit sought from the use of deferred preemption, which aids time composability. This work does not aim at reducing the explicit and hidden costs of a context switch (as done, for example, in [7,14,19]); our objective instead is that of enabling the adoption of a deferred preemption model that understands and covers the effects of resource sharing. In the following we first motivate and introduce our experimental objectives and set-up; we then assess the effectiveness of our approach and comment on the observed results.

div.head: Objectives and setup
div.p: Our experiments had a twofold goal. First we wanted to confirm the expectations on our approach and evaluate both correctness and effectiveness of the extensions we propose to the deferred preemption model. To this end we compared our solution, which is based on a safe interaction of NPRS and cs, against a standard fully preemptive model, implement ing a resource access protocol. We expected our approach to incur less preemptions, while at the same time provid ing the same guarantees on mutual exclusion. Secondly, we also wanted to compare the more conservative model-level solution with the respective run-time optimization, to evalu ate the effectiveness of our solution in avoiding unnecessary preemptions and size the degree of pessimism in the model. Unfortunately, no comparison is possible between our so lution and the original activation-triggered model since we cannot integrate critical sections in the latter, as we already observed in Section 3.

We are particularly interested in the practical applicabil-ity of our approach and attach much value to the representa tiveness of the experiments. For this reason we decided not to resort to model simulation and opted for implementing and evaluating our solutions on top of a full-fledged real time kernel instead. We integrated our deferred preemp tion model in ORK+ [25], an open-source real-time kernel of small size and complexity, especially suited for mission critical space applications 3 . Moreover the PowerPC port of ORK+ is characterized by constant-time OS services and low-interference time management [3], which are expected, among others, to enable OS-level time composability and to improve the accuracy of dynamic measurements. The choice of ORK+ was also guided by the fact that it complies with the Ravenscar profile [12], a standardised subset of the Ada language that specifies a reduced task ing model where all language constructs that are exposed to non-determinism or unbounded execution cost are categori cally excluded. Its most relevant feature, for the purpose of this work, is that the profile forces task communication and synchronization via critical sections under ICPP.

We conducted our experiments on top of a highly-configu rable SocLib-based PowerPC 750 [15] simulation platform. This allowed us to implement a zero-overhead instrumenta tion mechanism to gather experimental data. As a common experimental set-up, we configured the simulator to operate with both instruction and data cache disabled so as to level the costs of preemptions and avoid jittery timing behaviour in the application tasks.

div.head: Assessment
div.p: We performed our experiments on randomly generated task sets with increasing overall system utilization, ranging in between 20% and 90%4• Single task utilizations were gen erated according to a random uniform distribution within the range [0.001, 0. 1]. Tasks were also constrained to ex hibit integral harmonic periods uniformly distributed within the [10ms, 250ms] range, so as to keep the experiment size manageable and to have full understanding of task inter actions on shared resources. With respect to the effect of shared resources, we wanted our experiments to consider ably vary also on number, duration and relative position (within the task body) of critical sections in the system. In order to avoid an explosion in the possible scenarios we fo cused on the worst-case setting were all tasks share the one and the same resource and thus compete for the same (sys tem) ceiling. The cs duration, instead, is expressed as a fraction of the maximum allowed blocking (which also cor responds to qmax) and varies within 25% and 100% of the latter. The relative position of the cs accessing the shared resource is randomly determined following a uniform distri bution with range [0, 1], the extreme ends of which stand for the beginning and the end of task body respectively. All the experimental scenarios were verified to be feasible by RTA (accounting for kernel overheads) and where confirmed to be so by run-time monitoring in the kernel.
Our first set of experiments had a twofold objective. As an initial step, we wanted to ascertain the soundness of our approach with respect to shared resource access protection.

Then, we wanted to assess whether our limited-preemptive scheduling approach in the presence of shared resources still allows a reduction in the number of preemptions, as the state-of-art-model does. We instrumented the kernel to in tercept potential deadline misses and to count the number of preemptions globally incurred by all tasks in a task set during its hyper-period. We collected the run-time traces of more than 100 randomly generated task sets per each utiliza tion level in the range 20-90%. Each task set was character ized by a random combination of cs durations and relative position within each task. Figure 6 compares our imple mentation against the fully-preemptive scheduler provided by ORK+. The graph herein reports maximum and mini mum number of preemptions cumulatively incurred in a task set for each utilization level by FP, LP _MOD and LP _RT, respec tively the baseline deferred-preemption model accounting for shared resources and its run-time optimization.

div.p: As a preliminary observation, we note that the absence of deadline misses confirms that our implementation of Iimited preemptive scheduling provides a sound protection mecha nism for shared resources. Focusing on each algorithm sep arately, we observe that the number of preemptions in a task set simply increases with the total utilization. This is in part due to the way the task sets were generated, as greater utilisations are obtained by increasing the size of the task set. However, higher utilization levels (with rela tively small tasks) typically entails more complex task in terleaving and thus more preemptions. The most impor tant observation that can be made from Figure 6 is that, in accordance to state-of-the-art results on limited-preemptive scheduling, also in the presence of shared resources, Iimited preemptive schedulers generally outperforms the fully pre emptive one. As expected, even the basic LP _MOD scheduler performs slightly better than the FP algorithm in approxi mately achieving a 5% uniform reduction in the number of preemptions in medium-and high-utilization task sets. No remarkable gain can be observed instead at extremely low utilization levels (Le. , 20%). Besides proving the validity of our basic model Figure 6 also provides evidence of the improvement achievable at run time by adopting the opti mizations described in Section 4.2. As observed in Section 4, a simple-minded extension of the limited-preemptive model to account for shared resources may incur some unnecessary preemptions. Data are extracted from the same set of experiments re ported by Figure 6. They represent those task sets per uti lization for which we observed the maximum reduction in the number of preemptions for both variants. The number of preemptions incurred with LP _RT (the right-most bar of any triplet) is always no worse than what observed without it, for any scenario and any utilization rate. This difference with respect FP and LP _MOD is increasingly more evident as the task set utilization grows.

We finally investigated how the total number of preemp tions incurred by the task set in a hyperperiod varies as a consequence of increasing the duration of blocking caused by resource sharing. To this end we gradually increased the duration of the critical sections (proportionally to each task duration) so as to cause larger blocking on higher-priority tasks. Figure 8 shows the results of a comparison between fully-preemptive (FP) and our limited-preemptive variants LP _MOD) and LP _ RT on the number of preemptions incurred when the size of such critical section ranges over a repre sentative set of equivalence classes (namely 25, 50, 75 and 100% of the theoretically admissible blocking derived from the computation of qmax) , under increasing task set utilisa tion. The results confirm the goodness of the LP _RT imple mentation which incurs always less preemptions than those observed under the other settings. In addition, whereas the preemptions suffered by LP _ MOD slightly increase with larger critical sections, the LP _RT solutions always incurs a con stant number of preemptions, regardless of the duration of the critical section.

div.head: CONCLUSION
div.p: In the presence of history-sensitive hardware, task pre emption incurs increasingly relevant inter-task interference, wrecking the assumption of time composability, which stands at the base of state-of-the-art schedulability analysis ap proaches. Non-preemptive regions in deferred preemption approaches intuitively reduce the amount of inter-task inter ference as an effect of limiting the number of preemptions. When tasks share resources in mutual exclusion, however, the interactions between non-preemptive regions and criti cal sections exposes some flaws in the model.

In this paper we proposed a model extension that al lows accommodating critical sections within the activation triggered deferred preemption approach. Our extension is conservative in the sense that it benefits from the deferred preemption model with guarantees of not compromising the task set feasibility. We evaluated two variants of our ap proach, a basic version and a more optimised one, and show that they are both effective for allowing protected access to shared resources as well as reducing preemptions. The opti mized solution, in particular, proved robust against variabil ity in the duration and extent of sharing of critical sections.

Our immediate future work is to further extend our inves tigation to address preemption costs, in addition to preemp tion frequency, although we are aware that preemption cost and resource protection are quite orthogonal dimensions; and the latter cannot be renounced. We are also interested in studying the effects of phasing between non-preemptive regions and critical sections, as it intuitively impacts on the pessimism incurred by the model.
